course.summary: An undergraduate module covering simple and multiple regression with OLS and t test inference, using R and real datasets.
course.brief: Introductory econometrics for second-year economics undergraduates. A four-week module of weekly 90-minute lectures. Students know basic calculus and probability. Cover simple and multiple regression with OLS, then inference with t tests. Main text: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics. Assessment: weekly problem sets (30%), a midterm (30%) and a final exam (40%). Problem sets use real datasets in R.

l_94b7114dafd1.title: Simple regression and OLS estimation
l_94b7114dafd1.summary: Introduces the simple linear regression model and derives the OLS estimator from first principles.
readings: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, chapter 2 (The Simple Regression Model)
suggestedReadings: Stock and Watson, Introduction to Econometrics, chapter 4 (Linear Regression with One Regressor)

segments.title: Setting up the simple regression model
segments.description:
State the population model y = β₀ + β₁x + u and the sample regression line ŷ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x.
Explain that OLS chooses β̂₀ and β̂₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals, Σ(yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁xᵢ)².
Draw a scatter of a small dataset on the board and sketch several candidate lines to motivate why one line fits best.
Link this to the assumptions in chapter 2 of Wooldridge (SLR.1–SLR.4) that justify treating u as unrelated to x on average.
segments.teacherNotes: Common confusion: students think OLS minimises absolute residuals, not squared ones. Emphasise squaring avoids cancellation of positive and negative residuals and penalises large errors.

segments.title: Deriving β̂₀ and β̂₁ from the first-order conditions
segments.description:
Differentiate the sum of squared residuals with respect to β̂₀ and β̂₁ and set both derivatives to zero.
Show that the first condition gives ȳ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x̄, so residuals average to zero.
Show that the second condition gives β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², the ratio of sample covariance to sample variance.
Substitute back to get β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄.
segments.teacherNotes: Watch for sign errors when differentiating the square. Some students forget the chain rule factor of −1 and −xᵢ. Remind them β̂₁ is undefined if x has no variation.

segments.title: Hand-computing β̂₀ and β̂₁ on a small dataset
segments.description:
Give students a five- or six-observation dataset, for example hours studied and exam score.
Ask them to compute x̄, ȳ, the covariance sum and the variance sum by hand in pairs.
Have them calculate β̂₁ and β̂₀ and write the fitted line.
Circulate to check arithmetic and ask one pair to present their line on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect arithmetic slips in the covariance sum; check signs on (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ). A correct answer should give a positive slope if the scatter trends upward.

segments.title: Interpreting slopes across functional forms
segments.description:
Present three specifications: wage on educ, log(wage) on educ, and log(wage) on log(educ).
Ask students to state, in words, what a one-unit or one-percent change in educ implies for wage in each case.
Draw out that in log(wage) = β₀ + β₁educ + u, β̂₁ scaled by 100 gives an approximate percentage change in wage per extra year of education.
Discuss why economists often prefer log(wage) specifications for earnings data.
segments.teacherNotes: Students often say the log-level coefficient ‘is’ the percentage change rather than an approximation; the exact change is 100(e^{β̂₁} − 1)%. Clarify elasticity only applies when both variables are logged.

segments.title: Estimating the model in R
segments.description:
Load the wage1 dataset and run `lm(wage ~ educ, data = wage1)`.
Compare the R output slope and intercept with the same specification estimated in log form, `lm(log(wage) ~ educ, data = wage1)`.
Ask students to extract and interpret the coefficient on educ from the log specification.
Have students check that `summary()` gives the R² and compare it across the two specifications.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect the log specification’s educ coefficient to be roughly 0.08–0.09 depending on the sample. Remind students this is an association, not a causal effect, since ability is omitted.

segments.title: Quick check: reading R² and residuals
segments.description:
Ask students individually to answer two questions: what does an R² of 0.20 mean here, and why does a low R² not mean the coefficient is wrong.
Take verbal answers from two or three students and correct any misreadings.
Pose a follow-up: does adding an irrelevant variable to R ever lower R².
segments.teacherNotes: Target error from the reading: treating R² as the share of the causal effect explained. R² never falls when adding a regressor to the same sample; it can only rise or stay flat.

segments.title: Summary and link forward
segments.description:
Recap the two first-order conditions and the resulting formulas for β̂₀ and β̂₁.
Restate the three interpretation rules for levels, log-levels and log-log models.
Flag that the next topic extends this to several regressors using matrix algebra.
Remind students the problem set requires estimating and interpreting a simple regression in R.

keyIdeas: The OLS estimator is the unique intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals, obtained by setting two first-order conditions to zero
β̂₁ is a ratio of the sample covariance of x and y to the sample variance of x, and β̂₀ follows from the condition that residuals average to zero
The interpretation of β̂₁ depends on functional form: levels-on-levels gives units of y per unit of x, log(y)-on-x gives an approximate percentage change, log(y)-on-log(x) gives an elasticity
R² measures the share of variation in y explained by the fitted line, not the share of a causal effect explained, and a low R² does not imply biased estimates

vocabulary.definition: The estimation method that chooses β̂₀ and β̂₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals.
The difference ûᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ between an observed value and the value fitted by the regression line.
An equation obtained by setting the derivative of the objective function to zero, used here to derive β̂₀ and β̂₁.
Σûᵢ², the quantity OLS minimises when fitting a regression line.
β̂₁, the estimated change in ŷ associated with a one-unit change in x.
The proportion of the total variation in y explained by the fitted regression line, ranging from 0 to 1.
A model regressing log(y) on log(x), where the slope coefficient is interpreted as an elasticity.
The percentage change in y associated with a one percent change in x, given directly by the slope in a log-log model.

study.overview: This guide reviews how ordinary least squares (OLS) finds the best-fitting line through data, how to interpret slope coefficients under different functional forms, and how to read basic output from `lm()` in R. Use it alongside Wooldridge chapter 2 to consolidate the derivation and worked example covered in class.

points.heading: Deriving the OLS estimator
points.explanation: OLS chooses β̂₀ and β̂₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁xᵢ)². Setting the partial derivatives with respect to β̂₀ and β̂₁ to zero gives two first-order conditions. The first implies ȳ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x̄, so the fitted residuals average to zero. The second implies β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², the ratio of the sample covariance of x and y to the sample variance of x. Substituting into the first condition gives β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄. Practise this on the hours-studied and exam-score dataset from class: compute x̄, ȳ, the covariance sum and the variance sum, then check your β̂₀ and β̂₁ match what your pair found on the board.

points.heading: Interpreting slopes across functional forms
points.explanation: The meaning of β̂₁ depends on how y and x are measured. In a levels-on-levels model such as wage = β₀ + β₁educ + u, β̂₁ gives the change in wage, in pounds, for one more year of education. In a log-levels model such as log(wage) = β₀ + β₁educ + u, β̂₁ × 100 gives the approximate percentage change in wage for one more year of education; this is why economists favour this specification for earnings, since wage effects are often proportional rather than fixed in pounds. In a log-log model such as log(wage) = β₀ + β₁log(educ) + u, β̂₁ is an elasticity: the percentage change in wage for a 1% change in educ.

points.heading: Reading R² correctly
points.explanation: R² measures the share of the sample variation in y explained by the fitted line, not the share of a causal effect explained. An R² of 0.20 means the regression line accounts for 20% of the variation in y across observations, no more and no less. A low R² does not mean the coefficient is biased or wrong: β̂₁ can be an unbiased, well-estimated effect even when x explains little of the overall variation in y, because much of that variation comes from other factors captured in u. Note also that adding any variable to a regression, relevant or not, cannot lower R², since OLS can always set its coefficient to zero if it does not help fit.

points.heading: Estimating and comparing models in R
points.explanation: The command `lm(wage ~ educ, data = wage1)` estimates the levels-on-levels model and reports an intercept and a slope in pounds per year of education. Running `lm(log(wage) ~ educ, data = wage1)` instead estimates the log-levels model; the coefficient on educ, when multiplied by 100, is the approximate percentage wage change per extra year of schooling. Use `summary()` on each fitted object to extract R² and compare how much variation each specification explains. When you write up the problem set, report both the estimated equation and a one-sentence interpretation of the slope in the units implied by the specification you used.

l_3083987c7fc4.title: Multiple regression: estimation in matrix form
l_3083987c7fc4.summary: Extends OLS to several regressors, writing the model as y = Xβ + u and estimating β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y.
readings: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, chapter 3 (Multiple Regression Analysis: Estimation)
Week 3 notes: OLS in matrix form

segments.title: Opening discussion on chapter 3 and the week 3 notes
segments.description:
Students discuss why Wooldridge motivates multiple regression before showing the matrix form.
Ask them to explain, in their own words, why simple regression can give a biased picture when an omitted variable is correlated with the included regressor.
Use the wage1 example: what happens to the education coefficient if experience is left out.
Let two or three students respond before the tutor adds anything.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect the answer: omitted correlated variables bias the simple regression slope. Correct any student who says omission always biases upward; sign depends on correlations.

segments.title: Setting up the model in matrix notation
segments.description:
Write y = Xβ + u on the board, labelling dimensions: y is n × 1, X is n × (k+1), β is (k+1) × 1, u is n × 1.
Show the wage1 example with y = log(wage) and columns of X for the constant, educ, exper and tenure.
Explain why the first column of X is a column of ones.
Point out that each row of X is one observation, each column one variable.
segments.teacherNotes: Students often forget the constant column, which corresponds to β₀. Stress that n = 526 for wage1.

segments.title: Deriving β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y
segments.description:
Derive the normal equations from minimising the sum of squared residuals u’u = (y − Xβ)’(y − Xβ).
Differentiate with respect to β and set the gradient to zero to get X’Xβ̂ = X’y.
Solve for β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y and state the condition for this inverse to exist: X must have full column rank, meaning no perfect collinearity among regressors.
Relate this back to the week 3 notes definition.
segments.teacherNotes: Common error: thinking any high correlation between regressors blocks estimation. Only exact linear dependence does; near-collinearity just inflates variances, covered later.

segments.title: Computing β̂ on a small worked example
segments.description:
In pairs, students compute (X′X)⁻¹X′y by hand for a toy dataset with n = 5 and two regressors, using given X′X and X′y matrices.
They check their answer against the wage1 regression result: log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure.
Ask students to identify which entries of β̂ correspond to which regressor.
Circulate and check for correct matrix inversion.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected numeric answer for the toy example should be given on a handout. Watch for sign errors when inverting 2 × 2 matrices.

segments.title: Interpreting partial slopes with the wage1 example
segments.description:
Discuss what it means that the coefficient on educ is 0.092 in the wage1 regression.
Ask students to state the ceteris paribus interpretation: one more year of education is associated with about 9.2% higher wages, holding experience and tenure fixed.
Contrast this with the simple regression slope on educ alone, and ask why the two differ.
Invite students to propose another regressor that might belong in X and discuss.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect students to reference Wooldridge chapter 3 on ceteris paribus interpretation. Watch for the common error of ignoring the ‘holding fixed’ clause.

segments.title: Quick check on rank condition and interpretation
segments.description:
Pose two short questions: when does (X′X)⁻¹ fail to exist, and what does the coefficient on tenure mean in the wage1 equation.
Students answer individually, then compare with a neighbour.
Tutor takes verbal answers from the room rather than collecting anything written.
Clarify any remaining confusion before closing.
segments.teacherNotes: Correct answers: perfect collinearity in X; tenure coefficient means one more year of tenure is linked to about 2.2% higher wages, other regressors fixed.

segments.title: Summary and link to next topic
segments.description:
Recap the three objectives covered: matrix notation, the formula for β̂, and partial slope interpretation.
Preview that the next lesson examines whether β̂ is unbiased and how well the model fits, referencing the Gauss–Markov assumptions from the week 3 notes.
Remind students that the problem set requires estimating a multiple regression in R using a real dataset.
Answer any final questions from the discussion.
segments.teacherNotes: Confirm students know they will use `lm()` in R for the problem set, building on the wage1 example used in class.

keyIdeas: The multiple regression model is written y = Xβ + u, where X is n × (k+1) and its first column is a column of ones
The OLS estimator β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y minimises the sum of squared residuals and exists only when X has full column rank
Full column rank fails under perfect collinearity, for example when one regressor is an exact linear function of another
Each coefficient in β̂ is a partial slope: it measures the effect of one regressor holding all others in X fixed

vocabulary.definition: The matrix X of regressors, including a column of ones for the constant, with dimension n × (k+1).
The condition that no column of X is an exact linear combination of the others, required for (X′X)⁻¹ to exist.
An exact linear relationship among regressors that causes X to lack full column rank.
A coefficient in β̂ that measures the effect of one regressor on y holding all other regressors fixed.
The system X′Xβ̂ = X′y obtained by setting the derivative of the sum of squared residuals to zero.
The quantity u′u = (y − Xβ)′(y − Xβ) that OLS minimises to obtain β̂.
Latin for ‘other things equal’, used to describe the interpretation of a partial slope.

study.overview: This lesson generalised regression from one regressor to several, writing the model compactly as y = Xβ + u. You derived the OLS estimator β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y from first principles and practised interpreting its entries as partial slopes using the wage1 example: log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure.

points.heading: Matrix notation for the multiple regression model
points.explanation: The model y = Xβ + u packs all observations into matrices: y is n × 1, X is n × (k+1) with a first column of ones and further columns for each regressor, β is (k+1) × 1, and u is n × 1. In the wage1 example, X has columns for the constant, educ, exper and tenure, and each row is one worker’s observation. The column of ones lets the intercept β₀ be estimated alongside the slopes in a single matrix expression.

points.heading: Deriving and computing β̂
points.explanation: β̂ minimises the sum of squared residuals u′u = (y − Xβ)′(y − Xβ). Differentiating with respect to β and setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations X′Xβ̂ = X′y, so β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y. This inverse exists only when X has full column rank, meaning no regressor is an exact linear function of the others (no perfect collinearity). You practised this by hand on a small n = 5 toy dataset, computing (X′X)⁻¹X′y and checking that the resulting entries matched the pattern seen in the wage1 regression coefficients.

points.heading: Interpreting partial slopes
points.explanation: Each entry of β̂ is a partial slope: it measures the effect of one regressor holding all the others in X fixed. In the wage1 equation, the coefficient 0.092 on educ means one more year of education is associated with about 9.2% higher wages, holding experience and tenure fixed. This differs from a simple regression of log(wage) on educ alone, which would absorb some of the effect of experience and tenure into the education coefficient if these are correlated with educ, as chapter 3 discusses for omitted variable bias.

points.heading: Common pitfalls
points.explanation: Do not confuse the rank condition with anything about bias or fit: (X′X)⁻¹ fails to exist only under perfect collinearity, for example if one regressor were defined as twice another. Separately, remember that a low R² does not mean the estimates are biased, and R² should not be read as the share of any single regressor’s ‘effect’ that is explained; it only measures how much of the variation in y the whole model captures.

l_db32074fff6e.title: Properties of OLS: unbiasedness, Gauss–Markov and fit
l_db32074fff6e.summary: Covers the Gauss–Markov assumptions, unbiasedness, BLUE, and correct use of R².
readings: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, chapter 3 (Multiple Regression Analysis: Estimation)
Week 3 notes: OLS in matrix form
suggestedReadings: Angrist and Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, chapter 3 (Making Regression Make Sense)

segments.title: Recap: the five assumptions
segments.description:
Ask students to state MLR.1 to MLR.5 from memory, drawing on Wooldridge chapter 3.
Cold-call three students, one assumption each.
Write the five assumptions on the board as a checklist.
segments.teacherNotes: Common slip: confusing MLR.3 (no perfect collinearity) with MLR.5 (homoskedasticity). Expect precise statement of zero conditional mean, E(u|X)=0.

segments.title: From assumptions to unbiasedness
segments.description:
Present the two-step argument: MLR.1 to MLR.4 give unbiasedness of β̂, so E(β̂|X)=β.
Show the compact form from Week 3 notes, β̂=(X’X)⁻¹X’y, and explain why unbiasedness needs E(u|X)=0.
Stress that unbiasedness does not require MLR.5.
Set up the distinction between unbiasedness and efficiency, ahead of Gauss–Markov.
segments.teacherNotes: Sketch on board: β̂=β+(X’X)⁻¹X’u, so E(β̂|X)=β+(X’X)⁻¹X’E(u|X)=β. Keep algebra brief; focus on the logic, not full derivation.

segments.title: Why does homoskedasticity matter?
segments.description:
Seminar discussion led by students: what changes once MLR.5 is added?
Ask students to explain in their own words why Var(β̂|X)=σ²(X’X)⁻¹ needs homoskedasticity.
Push students to contrast this variance result with the earlier unbiasedness result.
Ask what would happen to inference if MLR.5 failed, without yet naming robust standard errors.
segments.teacherNotes: Students often think Gauss–Markov needs normality; it does not. BLUE means best among linear unbiased estimators, not best among all estimators.

segments.title: Gauss–Markov theorem: BLUE
segments.description:
State the Gauss–Markov theorem: under MLR.1 to MLR.5, OLS is BLUE.
Explain that “best” means minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
Note that BLUE only compares OLS with other linear unbiased estimators, not nonlinear ones.
segments.teacherNotes: Emphasise BLUE is a relative, not absolute, optimality result. Some students assume it means OLS is always the best possible estimator.

segments.title: Worked problem: wage1 data
segments.description:
Students work in pairs on the wage equation log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure from Week 3 notes.
Ask them to interpret the coefficient on educ and compute the implied wage change for four more years of education.

segments.teacherNotes: Key point: R² only measures explained sample variation; unbiasedness depends solely on MLR.1 to MLR.4. Low R² is typical with individual-level cross-sectional data.

slides.title: Properties of OLS: unbiasedness, Gauss–Markov and fit
slides.notes: Opening framing slide. Today we move from the mechanics of OLS in matrix form to its statistical properties: when is β̂ unbiased, when is it BLUE, and what does R² actually tell us. Draws on Wooldridge chapter 3 and the Week 3 notes on OLS in matrix form.

slides.title: Recap: MLR.1 to MLR.5
slides.notes: Cold-call three students, one assumption each, before revealing the full list. Write the five assumptions on the board as a checklist. These come straight from Wooldridge chapter 3. Note that MLR.3 is the full column rank condition mentioned in the Week 3 notes: X’X must be invertible.

slides.title: From assumptions to unbiasedness
slides.notes: Present the two-step argument: MLR.1 to MLR.4 give unbiasedness of β̂. Show the compact matrix form from the Week 3 notes, β̂=(X’X)⁻¹X’y, and explain why unbiasedness needs the zero conditional mean assumption. Stress that MLR.5 is not required here. This sets up the distinction between unbiasedness and efficiency for the Gauss–Markov theorem.

slides.title: Why does homoskedasticity matter?
slides.notes: Seminar discussion led by students: what changes once MLR.5 is added? Ask students to explain in their own words why the variance formula requires homoskedasticity, and to contrast this with the earlier unbiasedness result which did not need MLR.5. Ask what would happen to inference if MLR.5 failed, without yet naming robust standard errors; that comes later.

slides.title: Gauss–Markov theorem: BLUE
bullets: Not a comparison with nonlinear estimators
slides.notes: State the theorem formally. Explain that best means minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators of β. Emphasise the scope restriction: BLUE only compares OLS with other linear unbiased estimators, not with nonlinear or biased alternatives.

slides.title: Worked problem: wage1 data (n = 526)
slides.notes: Students work in pairs on this wage equation from the Week 3 notes. One more year of education is associated with about 9.2% higher wages, holding experience and tenure fixed. Ask them to compute the implied wage change for four more years of education. Then ask them to check MLR.3, full column rank, by inspecting X’X in R using `solve(t(X) %*% X)`. Circulate and check pairs’ working.

slides.title: R²: what it does and does not tell us
bullets: Low R² is common, not a problem
slides.notes: Open discussion on the common student error: reading R² as the share of the ‘effect’ explained, or treating a low R² as evidence of bias. Ask students to propose a scenario, using the wage1 example, where R² is low but coefficients remain unbiased. Ask why applied papers often report R² without treating it as evidence of causal validity.

slides.title: Quick check and summary
bullets: Growing variance with educ: violates MLR.5
Removing MLR.5 does not undo unbiasedness
Next: testing hypotheses with t tests

study.overview: This lesson established why OLS works: which assumptions make β̂ unbiased, which additional assumption makes it BLUE, and why R² is a measure of fit, not of correctness. Keep the assumptions and the fit measure conceptually separate, since students often conflate them.

points.heading: MLR.1–MLR.4 give unbiasedness
points.explanation: Wooldridge chapter 3 sets out MLR.1 (linear in parameters), MLR.2 (random sampling), MLR.3 (no perfect collinearity, full column rank of X), and MLR.4 (zero conditional mean, E(u|X)=0). Together these four are enough to show E(β̂|X)=β, using the compact form β̂=(X’X)⁻¹X’y from the Week 3 notes. Notice that homoskedasticity (MLR.5) plays no role here: unbiasedness holds even if the error variance changes across observations.

points.heading: MLR.5 and the Gauss–Markov theorem
points.explanation: Adding MLR.5 (homoskedasticity, constant Var(u|X)) gives Var(β̂|X)=σ²(X’X)⁻¹ and lets us invoke the Gauss–Markov theorem: under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE, the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator. ‘Best’ means minimum variance, but only among linear unbiased estimators — not among every possible estimator, and not necessarily against nonlinear alternatives. If MLR.5 fails, β̂ is still unbiased, but it is no longer guaranteed to be the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator, and standard inference formulas become unreliable.

points.heading: Reading the wage equation correctly
points.explanation: The estimated equation from wage1 (n = 526) is log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure. The coefficient 0.092 means one extra year of education is associated with about a 9.2% increase in wage, holding experience and tenure fixed. For four more years, the implied change is roughly 4 × 9.2% ≈ 36.8% (more precisely, e^{4×0.092} − 1). Checking MLR.3 in practice means confirming X’X is invertible, for example by running `solve(t(X) %*% X)` in R and checking it does not fail.

points.heading: R² measures fit, not truth
points.explanation: R² tells you the share of sample variation in y explained by the regressors — nothing more. A low R² in the wage1 regression is normal for cross-sectional wage data, since many determinants of wages (ability, effort, luck) are unobserved. This does not mean the coefficients on educ, exper or tenure are biased or inconsistent: unbiasedness depends on MLR.1–MLR.4, not on how much variation the model happens to explain. Avoid two common errors: treating R² as the ‘share of the effect’ explained, and treating a low R² as evidence against the model’s validity.

l_b6ce531d1119.title: Inference: t tests and confidence intervals
l_b6ce531d1119.summary: Introduces sampling distributions of β̂ under normality and applies t tests to coefficients.
readings: Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, chapter 4 (Multiple Regression Analysis: Inference)

segments.title: Reading discussion: inference in chapter 4
segments.description:
Students discuss the logic of chapter 4 of Wooldridge in pairs, then report back.
Focus questions: why does normality of u give a t distribution rather than a normal one for β̂_j, and why do degrees of freedom fall as k rises.
Ask students to explain, in their own words, what a standard error measures.
Collect one or two points of confusion on the board to return to later.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect confusion between σ² (unknown, estimated) and known variance; this is exactly why t, not z, applies. Some will conflate se(β̂_j) with σ̂.

segments.title: Deriving the t statistic and confidence interval
segments.description:
Derive t = (β̂_j − β_j)/se(β̂_j) from the normal sampling distribution of β̂_j and the estimated variance.
Show how setting β_j = 0 under H₀ gives the usual t statistic reported in regression output.
Derive the 95% confidence interval β̂_j ± t_{0.025,n−k−1} se(β̂_j) and show its link to the two-sided test.
Use the wage1 result log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure as the running example.
segments.teacherNotes: Emphasise degrees of freedom n−k−1 with n=526, k=3, so df=522, t_{0.025}≈1.96. Common error: using n instead of n−k−1.

segments.title: Testing the education coefficient in R
segments.description:
Students work in small groups using R on the wage1 data to fit `lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper + tenure, data = wage1)`.
They extract the standard error on educ, compute the t statistic by hand, and compare it to `summary()` output.
They then construct a 95% confidence interval for the education coefficient using `confint()`.
Groups test H₀: β_educ = 0 against a two-sided alternative and state their conclusion in words.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: t≈for 0.092 with se around 0.007, so t is large and clearly significant; CI should exclude zero. Watch for wrong df or wrong se column.

segments.title: Significance versus economic magnitude
segments.description:
Groups present their confidence interval for the education coefficient and discuss what it implies about the return to schooling.
Ask whether a coefficient of 0.092 that is statistically significant is also economically important, and what would make it unimportant.
Raise the common misreading that R² measures how much of the true causal effect is explained by education.
Link this back to the source note on common student errors around R² and bias.
segments.teacherNotes: Correct view: R² measures fit of the sample regression, not whether coefficients are unbiased or how large the true effect is; low R² does not imply bias.

segments.title: Quick hypothesis test
segments.description:
Give students a new coefficient and standard error, for example β̂ = 0.015 with se = 0.008 on tenure, and ask them to test H₀: β_tenure = 0 at the 5% level.
Students compute the t statistic and state a conclusion without using software.
One or two students explain their working to the group.
Correct any errors in reading the t table or degrees of freedom.
segments.teacherNotes: t = 0.015/0.008 ≈ 1.875; with df large, critical value ≈1.96, so fail to reject at 5% (borderline). Good example of near-significance.

segments.title: Summary and link to problem set
segments.description:
Summarise the three steps: state H₀, compute the t statistic, compare to the critical value or build a confidence interval.
Remind students that this week’s problem set asks them to test and interpret coefficients from a new dataset in R.
Flag the distinction between statistical and economic significance as a recurring theme for the midterm.

keyIdeas: Under MLR.6 (normality of the error term), β̂_j is normally distributed, so (β̂_j − β_j)/se(β̂_j) follows a t distribution with n−k−1 degrees of freedom.
The t statistic for testing H₀: β_j = 0 is t = β̂_j / se(β̂_j); reject at the 5% level if |t| exceeds the critical value from the t table.
A 95% confidence interval is β̂_j ± t_{0.025,n−k−1} se(β̂_j); it is the set of values not rejected by a two-sided test at the 5% level.
Statistical significance is not the same as economic significance: a precisely estimated coefficient can be significant but small in magnitude.

vocabulary.definition: The ratio β̂_j / se(β̂_j), used to test hypotheses about a single regression coefficient.
The estimated standard deviation of β̂_j, reflecting sampling variability of the OLS estimator.
n−k−1, the divisor used in estimating σ² and in choosing the critical value for the t distribution.
A range of values for β_j, here β̂_j ± t_{0.025,n−k−1} se(β̂_j), not rejected by a two-sided test at the stated level.
A hypothesis test where the alternative allows β_j to be either above or below the value in H₀.
The probability of observing a t statistic as extreme as the one computed, if H₀ were true.
A result unlikely to arise by sampling variation alone, judged by comparing the t statistic to a critical value.
The hypothesis being tested, typically H₀: β_j = 0, meaning no partial effect once other regressors are held fixed.

slides.title: Inference: t tests and confidence intervals
slides.notes: Open by linking back to chapter 4 reading discussion. Ask students why normality of u matters for inference, and what a standard error measures. Collect points of confusion on the board to revisit later in the session.

slides.title: Why a t distribution, not a normal one?
bullets: Why does normality of u give t, not z?
Why do degrees of freedom fall as k rises?
What does a standard error measure?
slides.notes: Use these as focus questions for the paired discussion on chapter 4. Encourage students to explain in their own words before offering the formal answer: β̂_j is a linear function of normal errors, so it is normal, but we must estimate σ² separately, introducing extra sampling variation captured by the t distribution with n−k−1 degrees of freedom.

slides.title: The t statistic for H₀: βⱼ = 0
slides.notes: Derive t = (β̂_j − β_j)/se(β̂_j) from the sampling distribution of β̂_j. Setting β_j = 0 under H₀ gives the usual t statistic reported in regression output. Emphasise degrees of freedom n−k−1, where k is the number of regressors.

slides.title: The 95% confidence interval
bullets: Values not rejected by a two-sided test
Same information as the t test, reframed
slides.notes: Show the link between the confidence interval and the two-sided test: any value inside the interval would not be rejected at the 5% level. Use the wage1 result log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure as the running example throughout.

slides.title: Testing educ in R
bullets: Compute t by hand, compare to output
slides.notes: Groups work through this on the wage1 data. They should recover the coefficient 0.092 on educ, compute t = 0.092/se by hand, check against summary() output, then use confint() to build the interval. State the conclusion for H₀: β_educ = 0 in words, not just numbers.

slides.title: Significant, but important?
bullets: Does R² measure the causal effect explained?
slides.notes: Groups present their confidence interval for educ and discuss the implied return to schooling. Raise the common misreading that R² measures how much of the true causal effect is explained, and that low R² does not imply biased estimates. Distinguish statistical significance from economic magnitude.

bullets: No software, use the t table
slides.notes: Students compute t = 0.015/0.008 = 1.875 and compare to the critical value for the relevant degrees of freedom. Ask one or two students to explain their working. Correct any errors in reading the t table or in degrees of freedom.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Compare to critical value, or build a CI
Statistical vs economic significance recurs at midterm

study.overview: This guide consolidates how to test hypotheses about individual regression coefficients using t statistics and confidence intervals, building on the wage1 example log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure. Under MLR.6 (normality of the error), β̂_j is normally distributed, but because we must estimate σ² from the data, the standardised statistic (β̂_j − β_j)/se(β̂_j) follows a t distribution with n−k−1 degrees of freedom rather than a standard normal one. This matters for hypothesis testing and interval estimation throughout applied regression work, and for the midterm.

points.heading: The t statistic for H₀: β_j = 0
points.explanation: To test whether a regressor has any partial effect on y, compute t = β̂_j / se(β̂_j) and compare its absolute value to the critical value t_{0.025,n−k−1} for a two-sided 5% test. For the wage1 regression with n = 526 and 4 parameters, degrees of freedom are n−k−1 = 522, so the critical value is close to 1.96. In `lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper + tenure, data = wage1)`, the coefficient on `educ` is 0.092; if its standard error is around 0.007, t ≈ 13, far exceeding 1.96, so we reject H₀: β_educ = 0 at the 5% level.

points.heading: Why t, not z: the role of estimated variance
points.explanation: Normality of u (MLR.6) makes β̂_j normal, but se(β̂_j) is itself an estimate of the true standard deviation, computed from the residuals. This extra estimation uncertainty is what produces a t distribution instead of a normal one. As k rises, more parameters are estimated, degrees of freedom (n−k−1) fall, and the t distribution has fatter tails, meaning a slightly larger critical value is needed to reject H₀. In the wage1 example, moving from a simple regression (k=1) to the multiple regression with educ, exper and tenure (k=3) reduces degrees of freedom accordingly.

points.heading: Building and interpreting a 95% confidence interval
points.explanation: The 95% confidence interval for β_j is β̂_j ± t_{0.025,n−k−1} se(β̂_j). It contains exactly the values of β_j that a two-sided test at the 5% level would not reject. Using `confint()` on the wage1 model gives an interval for β_educ, for example roughly (0.078, 0.106) if se(β̂_educ) ≈ 0.007. Since 0 lies far outside this interval, this is consistent with rejecting H₀: β_educ = 0.

points.heading: Statistical significance versus economic significance
points.explanation: A coefficient can be statistically significant (t large, interval excludes 0) yet economically small, or vice versa with a large but noisily estimated coefficient. The educ coefficient of 0.092 implies roughly a 9.2% wage increase per extra year of schooling, holding exper and tenure fixed — both statistically significant and economically meaningful. By contrast, a hypothetical β̂_tenure = 0.015 with se = 0.008 gives t = 1.875, which does not clear the 5% two-sided critical value of about 1.96, so we fail to reject H₀: β_tenure = 0, even though the point estimate is not economically negligible. Remember also that R² measures the share of variation in y explained by the model, not the share of any causal effect explained — a low R² does not imply biased estimates.

t_b857b95d9c50.prompt: Wooldridge chapter 2 derives β̂₁ by minimising the sum of squared residuals rather than, say, minimising the sum of absolute residuals. What do we gain, and what do we lose, by choosing squared residuals as the criterion?
followUps: If a dataset has one extreme outlier in y, how would that observation distort β̂₁ differently under squared-error minimisation versus a criterion based on absolute deviations?
The first-order conditions ∑û_i = 0 and ∑x_iû_i = 0 fall directly out of the calculus. What do these two conditions mean in words, in terms of the residuals and the regressor?
Does minimising squared residuals require us to assume u is normally distributed? Why might students confuse the estimation method with the assumptions needed for inference?

t_fab12166dd1a.prompt: Suppose we regress log(wage) on educ and get β̂_educ = 0.092, versus regressing wage (in levels) on educ and getting a coefficient of, say, 60. Both regressions ‘use the same data’. Can both interpretations be simultaneously useful, or does one specification dominate the other?
followUps: How would you explain the 9.2% interpretation to someone who has only met percentages in accounting, not in growth rates?
What features of wage data (their distribution, their range) might make economists prefer the log specification on empirical grounds, not just convenience?
If a student reports the level regression’s slope as ‘£60 more wage per year of education, i.e. 60%’, what exactly has gone wrong, and how would you correct the reasoning rather than just the number?

t_30127c9b53de.prompt: In the matrix model y = Xβ + u, the design matrix X includes a column of ones for the intercept. Some students argue that dropping the intercept and just letting all regressors ‘centre themselves’ is harmless if you’re mainly interested in slopes. Do you agree?
followUps: What happens to R² and the interpretation of residuals if you force the regression through the origin?
Can you construct a case using the wage1 example where omitting the constant biases the slope on educ?
Why does full column rank of X require that no column, including the ones vector, is a linear combination of the others?

t_21bc73f5f5d2.prompt: β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y exists only when X has full column rank, meaning no perfect collinearity among regressors. Some claim near-collinearity is just as fatal as perfect collinearity, since results will be unreliable either way. Others say it is a completely different problem. Who is right?
followUps: What actually breaks down algebraically if two regressors are perfectly collinear, versus what merely gets large if they are highly correlated?
In the wage1 model with educ, exper and tenure, which pair of regressors would you expect to be most correlated, and what would that do to standard errors?
Does near-collinearity bias β̂, or does it only affect precision? How would you check which is happening?

t_0cec474edb29.prompt: Wooldridge lists MLR.1 to MLR.4 as the assumptions needed for unbiasedness of β̂, with MLR.5 (homoskedasticity) added only for Gauss–Markov. Why does unbiasedness not require homoskedasticity, but efficiency (BLUE) does?
followUps: If Var(u|X) is not constant, is β̂ still unbiased? What breaks, and what still holds?
Our notes say Var(β̂|X) = σ²(X’X)⁻¹ under MLR.5. What would the variance formula look like without this assumption, and why does Gauss–Markov no longer apply?
Can you think of an economic example, such as household expenditure data, where you would expect variance of the error to depend on the regressors?

t_46c011e135ab.prompt: The notes warn that a low R² does not mean β̂ is biased. Suppose a regression of log(wage) on educ, exper and tenure gives R² = 0.32. A student claims this means the coefficient on educ is unreliable. Where does this argument go wrong, and what would make the coefficient actually unreliable?
followUps: What does R² actually measure, in terms of explained versus total variation in y?
Which assumptions, MLR.1 to MLR.4, if violated, would genuinely bias β̂_educ, and how is that different from a low R²?
If we added more regressors purely to raise R², what would happen to the precision of β̂_educ, and would that make the estimate more trustworthy?

t_5ce5feaaa1d7.title: Simple regression and OLS estimation
t_5ce5feaaa1d7.prompt: Estimate and interpret a simple regression using the wage1 dataset, then explain what OLS is doing and what R² can and cannot tell you.

By hand, using a small five-observation dataset of hours studied and exam score provided in the lesson, compute x̄, ȳ, Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) and Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², then derive β̂₀ and β̂₁ and write out the fitted line.

t_650f78a2ad69.title: Problem set: multiple regression in matrix form
t_650f78a2ad69.prompt: Using the wage1 dataset in R, set up and estimate a multiple regression in matrix notation, then interpret the results. This exercise contributes to the weekly problem sets component of assessment.
steps: Load the wage1 dataset in R and construct the matrix X with columns for the constant, educ, exper and tenure, and the vector y = log(wage).
Write out the dimensions of y, X, β and u for this dataset, stating n and k explicitly.
Compute X′X and X′y by hand or in R, then calculate β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y using `solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y`.

Write a short paragraph interpreting the coefficient on educ as a ceteris paribus effect, and explain why it may differ from the simple regression slope on educ alone.

t_9ee60fa8c9d6.prompt: Setting the first-order conditions for OLS to zero, ∂/∂β̂₀ Σ(yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁xᵢ)² = 0 leads to which condition on the residuals?

choices.text: The residuals sum to zero, so ȳ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x̄
The residuals are all individually equal to zero
The residuals are perfectly correlated with x
The residuals have the same sign as u in the population model

t_9ee60fa8c9d6.explanation: Differentiating the sum of squared residuals with respect to β̂₀ and setting it to zero gives Σ(yᵢ − β̂₀ − β̂₁xᵢ) = 0, which rearranges to ȳ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x̄ — the fitted line passes through the sample means and the residuals average to zero, not that each residual is zero.

t_28fe094f82be.prompt: Using the five-observation dataset of hours studied (x: 2, 3, 5, 4, 6) and exam score (y: 65, 70, 75, 78, 90), compute β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².

t_cfeebdb6d143.prompt: In the specification log(wage) = β̂₀ + β̂₁ log(educ) + u, how should β̂₁ be interpreted?

choices.text: As the number of pounds wage rises for each extra year of educ, holding all other regressors fixed at their means
As the elasticity of wage with respect to educ: a 1% increase in educ is associated with a β̂₁% change in wage
As the percentage change in wage for a one-year increase in educ, scaling β̂₁ by 100 as in the log-level case
As the percentage change in educ associated with a one-pound rise in wage, treating educ as the dependent variable

t_cfeebdb6d143.explanation: With both variables in logs, β̂₁ is an elasticity — a percentage change in x is associated with a β̂₁ percent change in y. This differs from the log(wage)-on-educ case, where β̂₁ scaled by 100 gives an approximate percentage change in wage per one-unit change in educ.

t_30dd38ffda55.prompt: An OLS regression can produce unbiased estimates of β₁ even when its R² is low.

choices.text: True
False

t_30dd38ffda55.explanation: R² measures how much of the sample variation in y the fitted line explains; it says nothing about whether the estimator is biased. Unbiasedness depends on the assumptions SLR.1–SLR.4 holding, not on how much variation is explained.

t_eb93bc736632.prompt: Write the R command to regress log(wage) on educ using the wage1 dataset, and state how you would interpret the coefficient on educ from this output.
t_eb93bc736632.answer: `lm(log(wage) ~ educ, data = wage1)`; the coefficient on educ, multiplied by 100, gives the approximate percentage change in wage for one additional year of education, holding nothing else constant since this is a simple regression.
t_eb93bc736632.explanation: The command estimates the log-level specification. t_7a203d34c87f.prompt: In the Gauss–Markov theorem, what does ‘best’ mean when we say OLS is BLUE?

t_0f843eb61daf.prompt: Under MLR.1 to MLR.5, why does Var(β̂|X) = σ²(X′X)⁻¹ specifically require homoskedasticity, rather than just the zero conditional mean assumption used for unbiasedness?
t_0f843eb61daf.answer: Because deriving the variance of β̂ requires the error variance to be constant across observations (Var(u|X) = σ²); without this, the errors could have different variances and the simple σ²(X′X)⁻¹ formula would not hold, even though E(β̂|X) = β would still hold.

Because the true error variance σ² is unknown and must be estimated by σ̂², adding sampling variation captured by n−k−1 degrees of freedom.

t_184c98ecd3e1.explanation: Standardising β̂_j by its true standard deviation gives a normal distribution, but in practice we replace σ with σ̂, and this extra estimation step introduces the t distribution with n−k−1 degrees of freedom, as discussed in the reading on inference.

f_0c7ed7bf37e4.question: Why do we minimise the sum of squared residuals rather than the sum of residuals themselves?
f_0c7ed7bf37e4.answer: The sum of residuals alone can equal zero even with a terrible fit, since positive and negative errors cancel out. Squaring penalises large errors and gives a unique, differentiable objective, so the first-order conditions ∂/∂β₀ and ∂/∂β₁ of Σûᵢ² produce a single solution: β̂₁ = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² and β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄.

f_a54216e6c375.question: How do I interpret β̂₁ when the model is log(y) on x versus log(y) on log(x)?
f_a54216e6c375.answer: In log-level form, log(y) = β₀ + β₁x, a one-unit increase in x is associated with roughly 100×β₁ percent change in y. In log-log form, log(y) = β₀ + β₁log(x), β₁ is an elasticity: a 1% increase in x is associated with a β₁ percent change in y. Wooldridge chapter 2 sets out these functional form interpretations in the section on units of measurement and functional form.

f_995fb88f9622.question: When I run `lm(wage ~ educ, data = wage1)` in R, what do the reported numbers actually correspond to?
f_995fb88f9622.answer: `(Intercept)` is β̂₀ and the `educ` row gives β̂₁, the estimated slope. The `Estimate` column matches the least squares formulas derived by hand; `Std. Error`, `t value` and the p-value belong to inference, which is not our focus here, but you will use them properly when covering t tests and confidence intervals.

f_f21f1d17191f.question: Why do we need X to have full column rank for β̂ to exist?
f_f21f1d17191f.answer: β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹X′y requires inverting X′X. If a regressor is an exact linear combination of others (perfect collinearity), X′X is singular and has no inverse. As the notes put it, β̂ exists only when X has full column rank (no perfect collinearity).

f_f8c460685c45.question: What does ‘holding other regressors fixed’ actually mean in the wage example?
f_f8c460685c45.answer: In log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure, the coefficient 0.092 on educ is the effect of an extra year of education on log(wage) when exper and tenure do not change. It is the partial derivative of the fitted equation with respect to educ, not a comparison across people who differ in everything at once.

f_102beacd49dd.question: Does a low R² mean our coefficient estimates are wrong or biased?
f_102beacd49dd.answer: No. R² measures the share of the variation in y explained by the regressors, not whether β̂ is biased. As passage [5] warns, a low R² can go with perfectly unbiased, well-estimated coefficients if the model is correctly specified; unbiasedness depends on MLR.1–MLR.4 holding, not on how much variance is explained.

f_b6ae02c50815.question: What exactly do MLR.1 to MLR.5 say, and which one is ‘the big one’?
f_b6ae02c50815.answer: MLR.1 is linearity in parameters, MLR.2 is random sampling, MLR.3 is no perfect collinearity, MLR.4 is zero conditional mean (E(u|X) = 0), and MLR.5 is homoskedasticity (Var(u|X) = σ²). As the Week 3 notes state, MLR.1–MLR.4 give unbiasedness of β̂; MLR.5 is added on top to get Var(β̂ | X) = σ²(X’X)⁻¹ and the Gauss–Markov (BLUE) result. MLR.4 is usually the hardest to satisfy and the one most threatened by omitted variables, so it does most of the work.

f_dcc5cc865e3e.question: What does ‘BLUE’ actually mean, and does it mean OLS is the best estimator full stop?
f_dcc5cc865e3e.answer: BLUE means Best Linear Unbiased Estimator: among all estimators that are linear in y and unbiased, OLS has the smallest variance under MLR.1–MLR.5. It does not mean OLS beats every possible estimator; a biased estimator could have lower mean squared error, and without MLR.5 (homoskedasticity) OLS is still unbiased but no longer guaranteed to have minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators.

f_3e12c62b15c0.question: If R² is low, does that mean our coefficient estimates are wrong or biased?
f_3e12c62b15c0.answer: No. As the notes warn in [5], this is a common student error. R² measures how much sample variation in y is explained by the regressors; it says nothing about whether MLR.1–MLR.4 hold. A regression can have unbiased, well-estimated coefficients with a low R² (much unexplained variation, e.g. individual wage variation not captured by educ, exper, tenure), and a high R² does not rescue a regression that violates zero conditional mean.

f_2fef9d7805c0.question: Why do we need the normality assumption (MLR.6) to do t tests, when Gauss–Markov didn’t need it?
f_2fef9d7805c0.answer: Gauss–Markov only needs assumptions MLR.1–MLR.5 to show OLS is BLUE, but that says nothing about the exact distribution of β̂ in finite samples. Adding MLR.6 (u independent of X, u ~ Normal(0, σ²)) makes β̂_j normally distributed, so (β̂_j − β_j)/se(β̂_j) follows a t distribution with n−k−1 degrees of freedom. Without normality, we’d need large-sample arguments instead.

f_0d5ec3756761.question: How do I read the t statistic for `educ` in the wage1 regression, and what does it tell me?
f_0d5ec3756761.answer: From log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure, the t statistic is β̂_educ divided by its standard error. If se(β̂_educ) is, say, 0.007, then t = 0.092/0.007 ≈ 13.1. Compare this with the critical value from t_{n−k−1} at the 5% level (roughly 1.96 for n = 526). Since 13.1 far exceeds this, we reject H₀: β_educ = 0 and conclude education has a statistically significant association with log(wage), holding experience and tenure fixed.

f_1cd075c8746b.question: What’s the difference between a coefficient being ‘statistically significant’ and ‘economically significant’?
f_1cd075c8746b.answer: Statistical significance just means we can confidently rule out β_j = 0 given the sample size and variability. Economic significance is about the size of the effect. Here, 0.092 means roughly a 9.2% wage increase per extra year of education, which is economically large. A coefficient could be statistically significant but tiny in magnitude, or large but imprecisely estimated with a wide confidence interval, so always report both the point estimate and its confidence interval, not just the t statistic.

# Week 3 notes: OLS in matrix form

The multiple regression model is y = Xβ + u, where X is n × (k+1) and includes a column of ones.

The OLS estimator minimises the sum of squared residuals and is β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y. It exists when X has full column rank (no perfect collinearity).

Under MLR.1–MLR.4, β̂ is unbiased. Adding MLR.5 (homoskedasticity), Var(β̂ | X) = σ²(X'X)⁻¹, and OLS is BLUE (Gauss–Markov).

Worked example (wage1 data, n = 526): log(wage) = 0.284 + 0.092 educ + 0.0041 exper + 0.022 tenure. One more year of education is associated with about 9.2% higher wages, holding experience and tenure fixed.

Common student error: reading the R² as the share of the "effect" explained, or thinking a low R² means the estimates are biased.
